It's the most widely used cross-platform mobile framework, backed by Meta and a massive open-source community.
subjects.body: Building separate native apps for iOS and Android traditionally meant learning two entirely different toolkits and often maintaining two separate codebases in parallel. React Native changes that by letting you write your app once, using React and JavaScript, while still rendering genuine native UI components on each platform, not a webpage wrapped to look like an app. This subject starts with React Native's core components — View, Text, and others that map to real native UI elements — and how they differ subtly but importantly from their web equivalents. From there, you'll cover navigation between screens, handling touch gestures and platform-specific behaviour, styling with React Native's Flexbox-based system, and connecting to backend APIs, much like you would in a web React app. You'll also learn to access native device features like the camera and location, and the practical realities of testing on both a simulator and real devices, along with understanding where platform differences between iOS and Android genuinely require separate handling. Because it reuses your existing React knowledge, React Native is often the fastest path for a web developer to start building real, published mobile apps without starting completely from scratch.

subjects.title: Computer Fundamentals
subjects.description: Computer Fundamentals covers the essential building blocks everyone should understand before using a computer confidently — hardware basics, how Windows works, files and folders, and simple troubleshooting. It's the true starting point for anyone new to computers, with no assumptions about prior experience.
subjects.body: Before learning any specific software or programming skill, it genuinely helps to understand the computer itself — what its main parts do, how the operating system organises everything, and how to navigate confidently instead of clicking around hoping for the best. This subject starts with the basics of hardware: what the CPU, RAM, and storage actually do, and how they work together every time you use a computer. From there, you'll learn to navigate Windows comfortably — the desktop, taskbar, and Start Menu — along with essential keyboard and mouse skills that make everyday tasks noticeably faster once they become second nature. You'll also cover file and folder management, understanding how files are organised and how to keep your own work tidy and easy to find, plus basics of storage and memory, working with everyday applications, and connecting devices like printers. A dedicated section on basic troubleshooting and network and security basics rounds things out, covering what to do when something goes wrong and how to stay reasonably safe online. This subject assumes absolutely no prior experience and is built for genuine beginners who want real, practical confidence using a computer for work, study, or everyday life.

subjects.title: Internet & Digital Skills
subjects.description: Internet & Digital Basics covers how the internet actually works, safe and effective browsing, email, and everyday digital communication tools. It's built for anyone who wants genuine confidence using the internet safely and productively, without assuming any prior technical background.
subjects.body: The internet is something almost everyone uses daily, but real understanding of how it works — and how to use it safely and effectively — is often patchy at best. This subject starts with the basics of what the internet actually is and how a web browser connects you to websites around the world, then covers practical browsing skills: using tabs, bookmarks, and search effectively, and recognising the difference between reliable and unreliable information online. From there, you'll cover email fundamentals — writing clear, professional messages, managing an inbox, and understanding email etiquette that applies whether you're communicating for work or personal reasons. A significant portion of this subject focuses on digital safety: recognising phishing attempts and scams, understanding why strong, unique passwords matter, and practising safe habits around personal information online. You'll also cover everyday digital communication tools, like video calls and messaging platforms, that have become essential parts of modern work and life. This subject is designed for genuine beginners and assumes no prior technical background, focused entirely on practical, everyday confidence rather than technical depth. By the end, you'll browse, communicate, and stay safe online with genuine, everyday confidence.

subjects.title: Microsoft Office
subjects.description: Microsoft Office covers the essential productivity tools used in virtually every office job — Word for documents, Excel for spreadsheets, and PowerPoint for presentations. This subject builds real, practical fluency in the tools most workplaces expect every employee to already know how to use.
subjects.body: Word, Excel, and PowerPoint remain the default productivity toolkit across most workplaces, and genuine fluency with them is one of the most universally useful professional skills there is, regardless of industry or job title. This subject starts with Word: formatting documents cleanly, using styles and templates consistently, and working with features like tables and mail merge that come up constantly in real office work. From there, you'll move into Excel, likely the most powerful and most underused tool of the three — organising data, writing formulas and functions, building charts, and using features like pivot tables to summarise and analyse data quickly instead of manually sorting through it. You'll also cover PowerPoint, focusing on building presentations that communicate clearly rather than just look busy, using slide design principles that keep an audience engaged rather than overwhelmed with text. Throughout, this subject emphasises practical, everyday use over obscure features — the skills that actually come up in real meetings, reports, and day-to-day office tasks. Whether you're starting your first office job or want to genuinely level up beyond the basics you've picked up informally, this subject is built to make you noticeably faster and more capable across all three tools. You'll also complete a small realistic project in each application, mirroring the actual tasks a new office employee is commonly asked to handle in their first weeks.

subjects.title: Data Entry & Productivity
subjects.description: Data Entry builds the speed, accuracy, and organisational habits needed to enter and manage data efficiently and correctly. Covering typing skills, spreadsheet basics, and data quality practices, this subject is practical training for any role where accurate, fast data handling genuinely matters.
subjects.body: Data entry might sound simple, but doing it well — quickly, accurately, and consistently over long stretches of work — is a genuine, practical skill that many roles depend on. This subject starts with typing fundamentals, building both speed and accuracy through proper technique, since typos in data entry can cause real downstream problems, from incorrect records to costly business mistakes. From there, you'll cover spreadsheet basics as they apply specifically to data entry: organising data into clean, consistent columns, using basic validation to catch errors before they're saved, and simple formulas that help verify data looks correct as you go. You'll also learn practical habits that experienced data entry professionals rely on — double-checking work systematically rather than randomly, spotting common patterns that indicate an error (like a misplaced decimal or duplicate entry), and organising your own workflow to stay accurate even during repetitive, high-volume tasks. This subject is intentionally practical and hands-on, focused on the real skills that make someone genuinely reliable and fast at data entry work, which remains a real and valued skill across office administration, research, and countless operational roles. By the end, you'll be noticeably faster and more accurate than when you started, with habits that hold up under real workload pressure.

subjects.title: Linux & Shell Scripting
subjects.description: Linux & Shell Scripting covers command-line fluency, file systems, permissions, and writing shell scripts to automate repetitive tasks. It's an essential skill for anyone working with servers, DevOps tooling, or any environment where the command line — not a graphical interface — is how real work gets done.
subjects.body: A huge share of the world's servers, and most professional development and deployment tooling, run on Linux, which means genuine command-line fluency isn't optional for many technical roles — it's a daily requirement. This subject starts with navigating the Linux filesystem confidently: moving between directories, finding and viewing files, and understanding how Linux organises everything as files, even things that don't feel like traditional files at first. From there, you'll cover permissions — who can read, write, or execute a given file, and why getting this wrong is a common source of both bugs and real security issues — along with managing processes, understanding what's actually running on a system at any given moment. You'll also learn shell scripting itself: writing scripts that automate repetitive command-line tasks, using variables, loops, and conditionals within a shell script, and combining commands together using pipes to build powerful one-line solutions to real problems. This subject is essential groundwork for DevOps, cloud engineering, and backend development roles, where working comfortably in a terminal, rather than a graphical interface, is simply how day-to-day technical work gets done. By the end, a terminal prompt will feel like a genuinely useful tool rather than an intimidating black box.

subjects.title: Monitoring & Observability
subjects.description: Monitoring & Observability covers how teams know what's actually happening inside a running system — metrics, logs, traces, and alerting that catch real problems before users notice them. It's a core practice behind reliable software, and essential for anyone working in DevOps or site reliability roles.
subjects.body: Once software is running in production, you genuinely need to know what it's actually doing — is it slow, is it failing for some users, is something about to break — and that visibility is exactly what monitoring and observability provide. This subject starts with metrics: numerical measurements over time, like response times or error rates, and how to build dashboards that make a system's health visible at a glance rather than something you have to dig for. From there, you'll cover structured logging, which turns scattered, hard-to-search log messages into organised, queryable records that make investigating an issue dramatically faster than searching through raw text files. You'll also learn distributed tracing basics, which help you follow a single request as it moves through multiple services in a modern, distributed system — invaluable when a slowdown could be happening in any one of several places. A significant part of this subject covers designing effective alerts: catching genuinely important problems early, without generating so much noise that a team starts ignoring alerts altogether, a real and common failure mode. Together, these practices are what separates teams who find out about outages from angry customers from teams who catch and fix problems before most users ever notice.

subjects.title: AWS Cloud
subjects.description: AWS (Amazon Web Services) is the largest cloud platform in the world, and this subject covers its core services — compute, storage, databases, and security — aligned with the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner exam. It's the practical, hands-on follow-up to understanding cloud concepts in general.
subjects.body: Amazon Web Services is the market-leading cloud platform, and knowing your way around its core services is one of the most practically valuable skills in modern software and infrastructure roles. This subject builds on general cloud computing concepts and gets specific: EC2 for virtual servers, S3 for scalable storage, and RDS for managed relational databases, covering not just what each service does but when and why you'd actually choose it for a real project. You'll learn AWS's approach to security and access control through IAM (Identity and Access Management), how billing and cost management work in practice, and how core AWS services fit together into a working, reliable architecture. This subject is aligned with the domains covered in the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner exam, making it a strong foundation whether your goal is that certification specifically or just genuine, practical AWS competence for a cloud or DevOps-adjacent role. Given how dominant AWS is across the industry — from startups to the majority of Fortune 500 companies — this is one of the highest-leverage, most transferable cloud skills you can build, and a common entry point into cloud engineering and DevOps career paths.

subjects.title: Web Foundation
subjects.description: Every website relies on the same invisible machinery: a request travels from your browser to a server and a response comes back. This subject demystifies that machinery — HTTP, domains, DNS, hosting, SSL, and databases — so you understand how the web works, and can put a website online yourself.
subjects.body:
The web feels like magic until you understand its plumbing. This subject starts with the fundamentals every developer, and every curious user, should know: what happens when you type a URL and press enter, why HTTPS matters, what a domain and subdomain actually are, and what your browser is really doing when you open a private or incognito window. None of this requires writing code — it's the conceptual foundation that makes everything else about the web make sense.

From there, the subject moves into the practical side: actually putting a website online. You'll learn how hosting works — the difference between shared hosting, a VPS, and cloud platforms — how DNS records point a domain to a server, how SSL certificates secure a connection, and why browsers block certain cross-origin requests through CORS. You'll also cover the basics of setting up a database for a live site, and when a CMS like WordPress makes more sense than custom code.

By the end, you'll be able to explain how the web works to someone else, and — more importantly — actually take a website from a folder of code to a live, secured, publicly reachable URL. This is foundational knowledge for developers, and hands-on operational skill for anyone who ends up responsible for keeping a site running.

subjects.title: Communication Skills
subjects.description: Communication Skills covers the English grammar, vocabulary, and everyday communication habits that make you clearly understood at work — from basic sentence structure to writing a professional email and explaining a technical idea without jargon. Built for genuine beginners through intermediate learners, with no assumptions about prior grammar knowledge.
subjects.body: Being technically skilled isn't enough if you can't explain your thinking clearly — in an email, a meeting, or a quick chat with a teammate. This subject starts at the true beginning: the parts of speech, basic sentence structure, and the verb tenses that make up correct, everyday English, along with the vocabulary you need to express yourself without constantly searching for the right word. From there, you'll tighten up the details that trip up even confident speakers — prepositions, articles, punctuation, and the small grammar mistakes that quietly undermine how professional your writing sounds. Once the fundamentals are solid, this subject moves into practical, workplace-specific communication: writing clear and well-toned professional emails, listening actively and asking good clarifying questions, contributing confidently in meetings, and explaining a technical idea to someone who doesn't share your background — without over-explaining or drowning them in jargon. A final section covers the etiquette of remote and cross-cultural communication, since most modern teams collaborate asynchronously, in writing, and across different backgrounds and time zones. This subject assumes no prior grammar training and is built for learners at genuinely beginner through intermediate levels, with the goal of making you clearly, confidently understood — in writing and in person — regardless of your role.
subjects.scope: Covers foundational English grammar and vocabulary (parts of speech, sentence structure, verb tenses, prepositions, articles, punctuation) and practical workplace communication (professional email writing, active listening, meeting participation, explaining technical ideas simply, remote and cross-cultural etiquette). Does not cover advanced or academic English (essay writing, literary analysis), spoken-accent or pronunciation training, or public-speaking/presentation-design skills in depth — those would be separate subjects. Learners also work through realistic workplace scenarios — rewriting an unclear email, choosing the professional response in a meeting, and simplifying a technical explanation for a non-technical audience — to build practical, applied confidence rather than abstract grammar rules.

subjects.title: Financial Literacy for Non-Finance Roles
subjects.description: Financial Literacy for Non-Finance Roles teaches business analysts and other non-finance professionals to read a P&L, balance sheet, and cash flow statement, think in terms of margin and cost structure, build and defend a budget, and judge whether an investment or business case actually makes financial sense — without needing an accounting background.
subjects.body: Business analysts sit between the business and the numbers every day — reviewing a budget variance, sanity-checking a business case, or explaining why a 'profitable' initiative still needs cash — yet most were never formally taught how to read a financial statement or judge a financial argument. This subject starts with the three statements every company runs on: the profit & loss statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement, and the core vocabulary that ties them together — revenue, margin, assets, liabilities, equity, and EBITDA. From there it moves into applied thinking: distinguishing fixed from variable costs, calculating a break-even point, building and defending a budget, and explaining a variance without hand-waving. The final section covers financial decision-making at the level a business analyst actually needs it: evaluating an investment with ROI, payback period, and NPV/IRR at a conceptual level, and building or critiquing a business case using sensitivity analysis and honest risk framing. No accounting coursework, journal entries, or tax law — just the financial fluency to read a statement, question an assumption, and hold your own in a numbers conversation.
subjects.scope: Covers reading and interpreting the P&L, balance sheet, and cash flow statement; core financial vocabulary (revenue, margin, assets, liabilities, equity, EBITDA); profitability and cost-structure analysis (fixed vs. variable costs, break-even); budgeting, forecasting, and variance analysis; and investment/business-case judgment (ROI, payback period, NPV/IRR, sensitivity analysis, financial risk framing) for non-finance roles such as business analysts, product managers, and project managers. Does not cover bookkeeping, journal entries, tax law, or formal accounting certification (CPA/CFA-level) material — those would be separate, specialist subjects.
